description_full: BYD Electronic (International) Company Limited, an investment holding company, primarily engages in the design, manufacture, assembly, and sale of mobile handset components, modules, and other products in the People's Republic of China and internationally. The company is involved in various businesses comprising smartphones, computers, new energy vehicles, AI computing infrastructure, smart home solutions, game hardware, unmanned aerial vehicles, 3D printers, Internet of Things, robots, communication equipment, and others. It also provides assembly services; and manufactures and sells smart products, as well as components for consumer electronics products. The company was incorporated in 2007 and is headquartered in Shenzhen, China. BYD Electronic (International) Company Limited is a subsidiary of Golden Link Worldwide Ltd.
ceo_bio: Mr. Nian-Qiang  Wang | CEO & Executive Director | Age 61 | Compensation: $1.7M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 162K people. Revenue per employee of $166K ranks in the bottom quartile among Technology peers. Each employee generates $14K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $61 per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 10× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (2/10). R&D investment of 2% of revenue (limited) signals commitment to product development and talent.
financial_summary: Byd Electronic International Co is a mid-cap technology business with a $5.8B market cap on $26.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +16% over the past three years, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at 11% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, and 6% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $2.2B in free cash flow — roughly 8 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 5.34× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage runs at 9.9×.

Shareholder yield of 3.9% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 66% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and profit capture is only 0.1× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 2% operating margin is roughly in line with the Technology median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.09x its revenue share).
It accounts for 0.6% of sector revenue and 0.1% of sector operating profit.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 533 companies in the universe; the top four hold 29% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 36% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 46% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 59% and a beta of 0.76, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.38 vs 5y 0.50), so read it loosely.
Trading is thin (about $14K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 43% in the 2020 crash and 53% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The stock trades 77% below its DCF fair value of $11.24, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 54%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $9.10 to $14.40 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Technology peers: P/E 18.4 vs 27.4, EV/EBITDA 0.1 vs 17.1 and P/FCF 2.6 vs 26.1 (sector median).
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 38.2% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 52.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 25.9% annual cash-flow growth, 27pp less than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 11% earns above the cost of capital of 8.0%, but the 3pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.27).
It runs a 6% gross margin and converts 8% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 10% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.4x equity multiplier).
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $1.0B.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 3.4, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 16.1% over 3 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
own: Insiders own 66.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 13%.
It returns 3.9% a year to shareholders (0.5% in buybacks and 0.8% in dividends).
people: With about 162,500 employees, each generates about $166K of revenue, 0.4x the Technology median.
That works out to $14K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.7M (10x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (2/10, lower is better).
